passage: Come, sit, and I will tell you something from when I was your age. Your Abhinav Uncle was ten, and we had a maths test. I saw my friend Irfan tilt his head to copy from my page. My heart was thumping. He was my best friend, but other children had studied all week. I slid my page away. That evening I told him, "If you copy again, I will not help you. It isn't fair to the others." He was angry for two days. Then he came to me before the next test and asked me to teach him fractions. We sat on my verandah until dark. He still says I could have been kinder about it.

qa.q: How old was Abhinav when the maths test happened?
qa.a: He was ten.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav's heart thumping when he saw Irfan copying?
qa.a: He felt torn between protecting his best friend and being fair to the other children who had studied all week.

qa.q: What could a child do if a friend keeps copying in tests?
qa.a: They could refuse to help, tell the friend it isn't fair, offer to study together, and speak to a teacher if it keeps happening.

qa.q: How did Irfan see it at first?
qa.a: He was angry for two days, probably feeling exposed and let down, though he later asked to be taught and still says Abhinav could have been kinder.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood loyalty-versus-fairness dilemma over a friend copying, and how he refused to help and urged the friend to stop.

passage:
"Mummy, a boy in the hall copied the whole answer sheet in the quiz," said Wasim, dropping his bag. "I don't even know him. It made me so angry I wanted to shout."

"Did you say anything?" asked his mother, Devika.

"I told the teacher after, quietly. She said she would look into it."

"That was sensible. Anything else?"

"I also told her that another kid whispered a spelling to his friend." Wasim looked at the floor.

Devika waited a moment. "What's the difference between those two things?"

"The whole paper takes marks from other people. A whisper is small."

"Then save telling for what really matters."

qa.q: Who did Wasim tell about the copying?
qa.a: He told the teacher, quietly, after the quiz.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he saw the boy copy the whole answer sheet?
qa.a: He was angry about the unfairness; he says it made him so angry he wanted to shout. 😠

qa.q: What would you advise Wasim about reporting small things?
qa.a: Keep reporting for things that really take something from others, and let small slips like a whispered spelling go or handle them gently.

qa.q: How might the other children feel if Wasim reported every whisper?
qa.a: They might feel watched and stop trusting him, so he could lose friends even though he cares about fairness.

grounding: A child feels indignation at a stranger's cheating and reports it, and is guided not to become an informer over small things.

passage: The other boys on the football field in Toronto laughed at Chen's lunch box and called his dumplings smelly. Chen's face went hot. He said nothing, and at recess the next day he sat behind the bookshelf in the library. He began saying his stomach hurt so he could skip football. On Thursday his classmate Oskar found him alone and sat down beside him. Chen told him, in a small voice, what had been said. Oskar said he should tell the teacher. The next time the boys started, Chen said calmly, "I like my lunch," and walked to the library door where Oskar was waiting. The teacher spoke with the boys later that week.

qa.q: Where did Chen sit at recess after the teasing?
qa.a: He sat behind the bookshelf in the library.

qa.q: Why did Chen say his stomach hurt?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and wanted to avoid the boys, so he made an excuse to skip football.

qa.q: What did Chen try that was better than fighting?
qa.a: He answered calmly, walked away and told a teacher with Oskar's support.

qa.q: What was it like for Oskar to find Chen alone?
qa.a: He probably noticed that Chen was hurting and wanted to help, and sitting down beside him made it easier for Chen to speak.

grounding: A child feels shame at teasing and withdraws, then answers calmly, walks away and gets support.

passage:
I sit behind Sahil in class. A boy from the next class keeps calling him "Stick" in the corridor, and on Monday Sahil went red and stared at his shoes. At lunch I heard him mutter that he wished the boy would drop his water bottle on his own foot, and worse things too. I don't know what he really meant. He did not do anything. On Tuesday I saw him stay behind after class and talk quietly to the teacher at the desk. Later the teacher went to the other class. Sahil looked tired, but his hands were not clenched like before. I hope the name-calling stops.

- Keerthana

qa.q: What name did the boy call Sahil in the corridor?
qa.a: He called him "Stick."

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling when he muttered about the water bottle?
qa.a: He was probably angry and hurt; Keerthana cannot be sure what he meant, but the muttering suggests he wanted the boy to feel bad too.

qa.q: What could Sahil do if the boy calls him names again?
qa.a: He could keep telling the teacher, stay near friends, and say out loud that he is angry to someone safe instead of picturing getting even.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel about watching all this?
qa.a: She seems worried and also relieved, since she noticed his anger but could not be sure of it, and was glad he went to the teacher.

grounding: A bullied child wants revenge; a classmate observes the anger and how the child tells an adult instead of retaliating.

passage: I am Maria. When I was eleven, a girl named Simran used to pull my plaits and laugh at my accent. I hated going to school. One afternoon I found her sitting behind the school gate, wiping her eyes. She said, "Nobody at home even asks how my day was." I stood there, and I understood something. It did not make me forgive the plaits. I said, "I'm sorry it's like that for you, but you cannot pull my hair." Then I told our teacher what had been happening. That is why I tell you: you can understand why someone is unkind and still keep your boundary.

qa.q: What did Simran use to do to Maria?
qa.a: She used to pull Maria's plaits and laugh at her accent.

qa.q: What did Maria realise when she saw Simran wiping her eyes behind the gate?
qa.a: She realised Simran might be hurting at home, which explained her behaviour, but Maria still did not think it excused it.

qa.q: Why did Maria still tell the teacher?
qa.a: Understanding Simran did not remove the need for a boundary, and the pulling and laughing still had to stop.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when Maria spoke kindly but firmly?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and a little relieved to be noticed, and she also heard that her behaviour had a limit.

grounding: An elder recalls realising a bully may be hurting at home, understanding without excusing and keeping a boundary.

passage:
Saturday. Jyoti and her younger sister Rehana fought over the last mango slice, and Jyoti told Rehana to stay out of her room forever.

Tuesday. Amma checked Rehana's homework first, and Jyoti shut her book with a bang and muttered that Rehana always got the attention. Rehana stuck out her tongue.

Sunday. At the park two older boys grabbed Rehana's kite and laughed. Jyoti was across the field, but she ran over. "Give it back. She's my sister," she said, and stood in front of Rehana until they dropped it. On the walk home Rehana whispered thanks, and by the gate they were arguing about who would hold the kite string.

qa.q: What did the two older boys grab from Rehana in the park?
qa.a: They grabbed Rehana's kite.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when Amma checked Rehana's homework first?
qa.a: She felt jealous and overlooked; she shut her book with a bang and muttered that Rehana always got the attention.

qa.q: How could Jyoti and Rehana handle the next fight over attention?
qa.a: They could each tell Amma what they need, such as a few minutes of her time, so the fights stay smaller.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Jyoti after the park?
qa.a: She probably sees her as both an annoying rival and someone who will stand up for her, since she whispered thanks even though they argued again.

grounding: Two sisters fight over things and attention at home, but the older one defends the younger outside.

passage: Note from Francis, church volunteer, Christmas Eve. During the carols Samir stood on his toes to see the crib, his mouth open at the candles. He sang the parts he knew, a beat late and loud, and hummed the rest. When the lights dimmed for the last hymn he stopped fidgeting and held his grandmother's hand tightly. Afterwards he asked me whether the star had really moved, and whether the animals had been cold. I said the stories say they were warm. He seemed satisfied, then told me, "I like it when everybody sings together." I did not explain more; he was taking it in his own way. I will invite him to help hang the star next year.

qa.q: What did Samir ask Francis afterwards?
qa.a: He asked whether the star had really moved, and whether the animals had been cold.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling during the last hymn, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt awe and belonging; he stopped fidgeting, held his grandmother's hand tightly, and said he likes it when everybody sings together.

qa.q: How could Francis support Samir's wonder as he grows?
qa.a: He could let Samir take part, like hanging the star, keep answering his questions simply, and welcome harder questions later.

qa.q: How might Samir's grandmother feel watching him?
qa.a: She was probably moved and happy to see him join in, since he held her hand tightly.

grounding: A child feels devotion, wonder and belonging at a festival service through songs, candles and stories.

passage:
In the school prayer hall before the science test, Raghav shut his eyes tight and whispered, "God, please give me good marks and I will skip video games for a week and never fight with my brother." Hemant, standing beside him, whispered, "What are you saying?"

"A deal," said Raghav.

Hemant shrugged. "I just say thank you for my pencil box and my family."

Raghav thought that was odd. The test was hard, and his mark was only middling. He was disappointed, but he kept away from video games all week anyway. On Friday, before assembly, he whispered again, and this time he said only, "Thank you for helping me finish the paper."

qa.q: What did Raghav promise to skip?
qa.a: He promised to skip video games for a week and never fight with his brother.

qa.q: What did Raghav want in return for his promises, and how does that show the way he thinks of prayer?
qa.a: He wanted good marks in return for his promises, a trade-like way of praying that is common at his age.

qa.q: What could Raghav try before the next test?
qa.a: He could still pray if it comforts him, plan his study time as well, and give thanks afterwards whatever the result.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Raghav's prayer?
qa.a: He might find it strange because his own prayers are about saying thank you, though he only shrugged and did not judge.

grounding: A child prays for exam marks in exchange for promises, and later begins to move toward gratitude.

passage: I watched my brother Chetan's friend Saurabh come to our Diwali puja. He left his shoes at the door as Chetan did and looked at the row of lamps for a long time. "What is that small plate for?" he asked, and Chetan told him. During the aarti Saurabh stood quietly with his hands at his sides. He did not join in the singing, and nobody minded. Afterwards he asked whether he could taste the laddu and how the lamps were lit. He told us they do things differently at his home. I cannot tell what he was thinking, but he looked as if he was trying to remember everything.

qa.q: What did Saurabh ask about the small plate?
qa.a: He asked what the small plate was for.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's quiet standing during the aarti suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed respectful and curious, since he stood still and watched, though the narrator cannot be sure what he was thinking.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do to keep this respect while learning more?
qa.a: He could keep asking politely, listen to the answers, and share how things are done at his own home. 🙂

qa.q: How might Chetan feel when Saurabh asks questions?
qa.a: He is probably glad and proud to explain, feeling that his home and festival are welcome.

grounding: A boy attends a friend's festival of a different faith, asks questions and respects the rituals.

passage:
Suraj stood still in the middle of the crowded bazaar. His mother's yellow scarf was gone. His chest felt tight, but he took a slow breath and looked around, then walked to the sweet shop.

"Bhaiya, I am lost. Can you help me call my mother?"

The shopkeeper, Wasim, crouched down. "Stay here by the counter. What is her number?"

Suraj said each digit slowly, twice.

Wasim dialled and held the phone out. "Suraj is with me, at the sweet shop by the clock tower."

"Stay right there," said a voice, shaky and fast. "I am coming."

"Okay, Mummy," said Suraj. "I am standing by the counter."

qa.q: Whose number did Wasim ask Suraj for?
qa.a: He asked for Suraj's mother's number.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he noticed the yellow scarf was gone, and what did he do?
qa.a: He felt scared, with a tight chest, but he took a slow breath and went to a safe person instead of running around.

qa.q: What would you advise Suraj to remember for next time?
qa.a: Stay calm, stay in one place near a safe adult like a shopkeeper, and say the parent's number slowly until someone can call.

qa.q: How might Suraj's mother feel when she hears his voice?
qa.a: She probably feels very relieved after worrying, and glad he stayed calm and found a safe person. ❤️

grounding: A child stays calm when lost, approaches a shopkeeper and repeats the parent's number.
